content_html:
HobbyLM-Embed-140M

An English text-embedding model built on a sparse mixture-of-experts encoder, trained from scratch: 140M total parameters, 36M active per token (excluding embeddings), 512-dimensional dense embeddings for search, RAG, similarity, clustering and classification.
HobbyLM by Fuel Labs

GGUF | MLX | Demo | Cookbooks | Ollama | GitHub | MTEB

Hugging Face's automatic "Use this model" snippets are not validated for HobbyLM-Embed. Use the snippets on this page, which were tested as written.

Highlights

  • Trained from scratch. The encoder started from random weights and was pretrained on 50B tokens. It was not adapted from BERT, ModernBERT or any other existing encoder.
  • Sparse inside, dense outside. Each token runs through 8 of 32 experts in every MoE layer, with 36M parameters active per token, excluding the embedding table. The output is an ordinary dense 512-d vector that works with any vector database.
  • Officially on MTEB. 62.33 on MTEB(eng, v2), all 41 tasks, scored through the loader merged into the mteb package.
  • Reads long documents. 512 tokens by default; set it to 2,048 and long-document search improves from 36.1 to 49.3 nDCG@10 on LongEmbed.
  • Runs where you are. Sentence Transformers on CPU or GPU, LangChain, LlamaIndex and Chroma, llama.cpp (GGUF), Ollama, and MLX on Apple Silicon.
  • Apache-2.0. Weights, model code and tools.

Introduction

Most small embedding models are adapted from an existing encoder. We wanted to build one end to end: the architecture, the pretraining, every embedding stage and the evaluation. HobbyLM-Embed takes the sparse mixture-of-experts design of the HobbyLM model family, makes its attention bidirectional, and trains it from random weights into a general-purpose English embedding model.

The encoder has 140M total parameters, with 36M active per token excluding embeddings, and produces a 512-dimensional dense vector. It is meant to be practical: it runs on a laptop CPU, plugs into the common RAG frameworks, and has GGUF, Ollama and MLX versions for running locally.

How to read these numbers

  • Retrieval tasks use query: / passage: prompts; every other task uses plain text.
  • Fine-tuning used the training splits of some MTEB tasks (never their test splits), and some training text comes from the same source corpora as some MTEB tasks. All of these are declared in the model's MTEB entry: 26 of 41 tasks, so MTEB lists the model as 36% zero-shot.
  • The final checkpoint was selected using MTEB scores.
  • Treat the benchmark mean as optimistic for domains the model has not seen, and evaluate on your own data.

Long documents

The model reads up to 2,048 tokens when you raise the input length (see Quickstart). On LongEmbed's four real long-document retrieval tasks:

LongEmbed task (nDCG@10) 512 1,024 2,048
NarrativeQA 16.15 16.54 18.16
QMSum 21.60 27.94 32.10
2WikiMultihopQA 48.09 55.14 62.30
SummScreenFD 58.41 74.16 84.77
Average 36.06 43.44 49.33
  • On synthetic tests where one fact is hidden in a 2,048-token document, accuracy@1 rises from 22% to 96% (passkey) and from 24% to 82% (needle). At 512 the model only sees facts in the first 512 tokens.
  • On MTEB(eng, v2) the 40-task mean is unchanged at 2,048 (63.16 → 63.14), but similarity between long news articles (STS22) drops by 1.7 points. That is why 512 stays the default and 2,048 is a one-line option for long-document search.
  • The final fine-tuning stage used inputs of at most 256 tokens; lengths beyond 2,048 are not tested.

Training recipe

Four stages, each starting from the previous one's weights. Data sources are described by type; mixtures, preparation details and training code are not released.

Stage What it teaches Data
1. Masked-token pretraining Language, from random weights (50B tokens, sequences up to 1,024) Filtered web text, educational and scientific documents, Wikipedia, StackExchange, synthetic question–answer text and code; deduplicated and decontaminated against the MTEB(eng, v2) test sets
2. Contrastive pair training What "related" means (about 20M pairs) Public question–answer, title–body, paraphrase and citation pairs
3. Distillation (short) Light alignment to larger embedding models Teacher-scored public texts
4. Supervised fine-tuning Task skills, with teacher-mined hard negatives Public labelled data for retrieval, NLI, paraphrase, classification and clustering, including MTEB training splits; synthetic training triplets

What mattered most:

  • Measuring correctly. Scoring in fp32 and averaging clustering over several seeds removed noise that was larger than the effects we were testing.
  • Matching training and use. Short prompts the model saw in training help; long unseen instructions hurt a mean-pooled model.
  • Choosing data by measurement. Testing pair sources one at a time showed that some popular sources made out-of-domain retrieval worse.

Quickstart

Sentence Transformers 

pip install -U sentence-transformers

from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer

model = SentenceTransformer("harims95/hobbylm-embed-140m", revision="ea708cee107818fa0c1871eebd26d82a1e3fb1aa",
                            trust_remote_code=True)

queries = ["how do vaccines work?"]
passages = [
    "Vaccines train the immune system to recognise a pathogen without causing the disease.",
    "The Eiffel Tower was completed in 1889.",
]

q = model.encode_query(queries)        # adds "query: "
p = model.encode_document(passages)    # adds "passage: "
print(q.shape)                         # (1, 512)
print(model.similarity(q, p))          # tensor([[0.6537, 0.2375]])
  • trust_remote_code=True is required: the MoE encoder is custom code shipped in this repo.
  • encode_query / encode_document (or prompt_name="query" / "passage") add the prompts. Typing them yourself gives the same vector; never do both.
  • For similarity, clustering and classification, use plain model.encode(texts).
  • Embeddings are L2-normalised, so cosine similarity equals the dot product.

Long documents (up to 2,048 tokens) 

model.max_seq_length = 2048

Use it for long-document search (contracts, transcripts, reports). Longer inputs are slower to encode; chunk anything longer than 2,048 tokens.

LangChain, LlamaIndex and Chroma

Every snippet below was run exactly as written on CPU, each in a new virtual environment with an empty Hugging Face cache, with the model pinned to revision ea708cee107818fa0c1871eebd26d82a1e3fb1aa. langchain-hobbylm, LlamaIndex and Chroma give the same vectors as Sentence Transformers (cosine 1.000000 on 2 prompted queries and 2 prompted passages, and on a 5,098-token passage at 2,048 tokens); langchain-huggingface does for single-line text (see its note). As everywhere, queries need query: and documents need passage: . The LlamaIndex and Chroma snippets use these texts (the LangChain snippets define them inline):

QUERIES = ["how do vaccines work?", "what is the capital of france"]
PASSAGES = ["Vaccines train the immune system to recognise a pathogen without causing the disease.",
            "Paris is the capital and largest city of France."]

LangChain

Recommended: langchain-hobbylm 0.1.1. It sets the query / passage prompts and pins the model revision for you. Tested 23 Nov 2026 (Linux, Python 3.12.16, new venv, empty Hugging Face cache): langchain-hobbylm 0.1.1, langchain-core 1.8.4, sentence-transformers 6.3.0, transformers 5.24.0, torch 2.15.0, huggingface-hub 2.4.0, numpy 2.5.5.

pip install langchain-hobbylm

from langchain_core.vectorstores import InMemoryVectorStore
from langchain_hobbylm import HobbyLMEmbeddings

embeddings = HobbyLMEmbeddings(revision="ea708cee107818fa0c1871eebd26d82a1e3fb1aa")

queries = ["how do vaccines work?", "what is the capital of france"]
passages = ["Vaccines train the immune system to recognise a pathogen without causing the disease.",
            "Paris is the capital and largest city of France."]

q = [embeddings.embed_query(t) for t in queries]   # "query: " prompt
p = embeddings.embed_documents(passages)           # "passage: " prompt
print("dims", len(q[0]), "norms", [round(sum(x * x for x in v) ** 0.5, 4) for v in q + p])

store = InMemoryVectorStore.from_texts(passages, embedding=embeddings)
for t in queries:
    print(t, "->", store.similarity_search(t, k=1)[0].page_content)

Output (real run):

dims 512 norms [1.0, 1.0, 1.0, 1.0]
how do vaccines work? -> Vaccines train the immune system to recognise a pathogen without causing the disease.
what is the capital of france -> Paris is the capital and largest city of France.

The vectors are identical to Sentence Transformers (cosine 1.000000 on both queries and both passages), with no "new version ... malicious code" warning. Long documents: HobbyLMEmbeddings(revision="ea708cee107818fa0c1871eebd26d82a1e3fb1aa", model_kwargs={"tokenizer_kwargs": {"model_max_length": 2048}}) (tested on a 5,098-token passage: 512-d, norm 1.0, cosine 1.000000 vs Sentence Transformers with max_seq_length = 2048).

Alternative: langchain-huggingface. Tested the same way: langchain-huggingface 1.2.3, langchain-core 1.8.4, sentence-transformers 6.3.0, transformers 5.24.0, torch 2.15.0, huggingface-hub 1.33.0, numpy 2.5.5.

pip install langchain-huggingface sentence-transformers

    model_name="harims95/hobbylm-embed-140m",
    model_kwargs={"trust_remote_code": True, "revision": "ea708cee107818fa0c1871eebd26d82a1e3fb1aa"},
    query_encode_kwargs={"prompt_name": "query"},
    encode_kwargs={"prompt_name": "passage"},
)

queries = ["how do vaccines work?", "what is the capital of france"]
passages = ["Vaccines train the immune system to recognise a pathogen without causing the disease.",
            "Paris is the capital and largest city of France."]

q = [embeddings.embed_query(t) for t in queries]
p = embeddings.embed_documents(passages)
print("dims", len(q[0]), "norms", [round(sum(x * x for x in v) ** 0.5, 4) for v in q + p])

store = InMemoryVectorStore.from_texts(passages, embedding=embeddings)
for t in queries:
    print(t, "->", store.similarity_search(t, k=1)[0].page_content)

Output (real run):

what is the capital of france -> Paris is the capital and largest city of France.

langchain-huggingface replaces line breaks with spaces before encoding, so multi-line documents get slightly different vectors than Sentence Transformers (cosine about 0.97 on our long test). Use langchain-hobbylm for identical vectors.

Long documents: add "tokenizer_kwargs": {"model_max_length": 2048} to model_kwargs (the setting takes effect: on the text it actually encodes, with line breaks replaced, the vector is identical to Sentence Transformers at 2,048 tokens).

LlamaIndex

Tested 23 Nov 2026 in a new venv with an empty Hugging Face cache: llama-index-embeddings-huggingface 0.9.0, llama-index-core 0.14.26, sentence-transformers 6.3.0, transformers 5.24.0, torch 2.15.0, huggingface_hub 2.4.0, numpy 2.5.5, Python 3.12, CPU. LlamaIndex sets its own prompts, so the model's prompts go in query_instruction (queries) and text_instruction (documents). The revision is pinned, so no "new version ... malicious code" warning appears.

pip install llama-index-embeddings-huggingface

from llama_index.embeddings.huggingface import HuggingFaceEmbedding
embed = HuggingFaceEmbedding(model_name="harims95/hobbylm-embed-140m",
                             revision="ea708cee107818fa0c1871eebd26d82a1e3fb1aa",
                             trust_remote_code=True, device="cpu",
                             query_instruction="query: ", text_instruction="passage: ")
q = [embed.get_query_embedding(t) for t in QUERIES]
p = embed.get_text_embedding_batch(PASSAGES)

print("dims", len(q[0]), "norms", [round(sum(x * x for x in v) ** 0.5, 4) for v in q + p])
for t, v in zip(QUERIES, q):
    scores = [sum(a * b for a, b in zip(v, d)) for d in p]
    print(t, "->", PASSAGES[scores.index(max(scores))])

Output (real run):

dims 512 norms [1.0, 1.0, 1.0, 1.0]
how do vaccines work? -> Vaccines train the immune system to recognise a pathogen without causing the disease.
what is the capital of france -> Paris is the capital and largest city of France.

The vectors are identical to Sentence Transformers (cosine 1.000000 on both queries and both passages). Long documents: add max_length=2048 to HuggingFaceEmbedding(...) (tested the same way on a 5,098-token passage: 512-d, norm 1.0, cosine 1.000000 vs Sentence Transformers with max_seq_length = 2048).

Chroma

Tested 23 Nov 2026 in a new venv with an empty Hugging Face cache: chromadb 1.5.9, sentence-transformers 6.3.0, transformers 5.24.0, torch 2.15.0, huggingface_hub 2.4.0, numpy 2.5.5, Python 3.12, CPU. Chroma's embedding function has no query/document setting, so the prompts are added to the texts: query: for queries and passage: for documents. The revision is pinned, so no "new version ... malicious code" warning appears.

pip install chromadb sentence-transformers

import chromadb
from chromadb.utils.embedding_functions import SentenceTransformerEmbeddingFunction
ef = SentenceTransformerEmbeddingFunction(model_name="harims95/hobbylm-embed-140m",
                                          revision="ea708cee107818fa0c1871eebd26d82a1e3fb1aa",
                                          trust_remote_code=True, device="cpu")
q = ef(["query: " + t for t in QUERIES])
p = ef(["passage: " + t for t in PASSAGES])
print("dims", len(q[0]), "norms", [round(float((v * v).sum()) ** 0.5, 4) for v in q + p])

# end to end: in-memory collection, cosine space
col = chromadb.Client().create_collection("demo", embedding_function=ef, metadata={"hnsw:space": "cosine"})
col.add(ids=["vaccines", "paris"], documents=["passage: " + t for t in PASSAGES])
res = col.query(query_texts=["query: " + t for t in QUERIES], n_results=1)
print("top result per query:", res["ids"])

Output (real run):

dims 512 norms [1.0, 1.0, 1.0, 1.0]
top result per query: [['vaccines'], ['paris']]

The vectors are identical to Sentence Transformers (cosine 1.000000 on both queries and both passages). Long documents: add tokenizer_kwargs={"model_max_length": 2048} to SentenceTransformerEmbeddingFunction(...) (tested the same way on a 5,098-token passage: 512-d, norm 1.0, cosine 1.000000 vs Sentence Transformers with max_seq_length = 2048). Chroma keeps one loaded model per model_name in a Python process, so create the 2,048 version in a new process, not after a 512 one.

device="cpu" can be dropped on a CPU-only machine or changed to "cuda".

3. Embed texts

The helper needs only Python 3 (standard library). It runs llama-embedding --pooling none and pools the way the model was trained: the mean of the text tokens, excluding the final end-of-text token, then L2 normalisation.

printf "what is the capital of france\n" > queries.txt
printf "Paris is the capital and largest city of France.\nThe mitochondria is the powerhouse of the cell.\n" > passages.txt
B=./llama.cpp/build/bin/llama-embedding
python3 hobbylm_llamacpp_embed.py --bin $B --model hobbylm-embed-140m-f16.gguf --mode query queries.txt > q.jsonl
python3 hobbylm_llamacpp_embed.py --bin $B --model hobbylm-embed-140m-f16.gguf --mode passage passages.txt > p.jsonl
cut -c1-120 q.jsonl
python3 -c "
import json
q=[json.loads(l) for l in open('q.jsonl')]; p=[json.loads(l) for l in open('p.jsonl')]
for d in p: print(round(sum(a*b for a,b in zip(q[0]['embedding'], d['embedding'])),4), d['text'])
"

Output:

{"text": "what is the capital of france", "embedding": [0.0119629, -0.0288813, -0.0404069, -0.0176782, 0.0519803, 0.0387
0.7309 Paris is the capital and largest city of France.
0.378 The mitochondria is the powerhouse of the cell.
  • --mode query / --mode passage for retrieval; --mode none for similarity, classification and clustering.
  • One text per line; texts are stripped. The GGUF files are tested at 512 tokens; their context limit is 1,024 tokens. For long documents (up to 2,048 tokens) use Sentence Transformers with model.max_seq_length = 2048. llama.cpp does not truncate, so shorten longer texts yourself.

llama.cpp's built-in mean pooling includes the end-of-text token, so use the helper script for exact embeddings.

Ollama 

ollama pull hariharanms95/hobbylm-embed-140m

curl http://localhost:11434/api/embed -d '{
  "model": "hariharanms95/hobbylm-embed-140m",
  "input": ["query: how do vaccines work?",
            "passage: Vaccines train the immune system to recognise a pathogen without causing the disease."]
}'

The response holds one 512-d, L2-normalised vector per input under "embeddings". As with the other runtimes, prefix retrieval queries with query: and documents with passage: , and use plain text for similarity, clustering and classification. The model runs with num_ctx 512.

Ollama's pooling includes the final end-of-text token, so its vectors are close to but not identical with the reference model: on normal sentences cosine is about 0.99 and task scores stay within ±0.4, but very short texts (one or two words) differ most (cosine about 0.92–0.97). Don't mix Ollama vectors with exact vectors in one index.

MLX (Apple Silicon) 

pip install mlx tokenizers numpy huggingface_hub

import sys
from huggingface_hub import snapshot_download

path = snapshot_download("harims95/hobbylm-embed-140m-mlx")
sys.path.insert(0, path)
from hobbylm_mlx import Encoder

enc = Encoder(path, quant_dir=path)
q = enc.encode(["what is the capital of france"], prompt_name="query")
p = enc.encode(["Paris is the capital and largest city of France."], prompt_name="passage")
print(q @ p.T)   # vectors are L2-normalised: this is cosine similarity

Long documents (up to 2,048 tokens):

enc = Encoder(path, quant_dir=path, max_seq_length=2048)

Limitations and disclaimer

  • English only. The GPT-2 tokenizer is also inefficient for code and non-English text.
  • Prompts matter. Retrieval needs query: / passage: ; mixing prompted and unprompted vectors in one index degrades results.
  • Input length. 512 tokens by default; up to 2,048 tested on LongEmbed; longer inputs are slower and nothing beyond 2,048 is tested.
  • Custom code. Loading requires trust_remote_code=True. The reference implementation runs experts in a loop, so batching texts together is much faster than encoding them one at a time.
  • Benchmark context. The MTEB score includes tasks whose training splits were used, and the checkpoint was selected on MTEB. Evaluate on your own data before relying on it.
  • No guarantees. Embeddings can reflect biases in public web and labelled data. The model is provided as is, without warranty.

Training recipe Four stages, each starting from the previous one's weights. Data sources are described by type; mixtures, preparation details and training code are not released. Stage What it teaches Data 1. Masked-token pretraining Language, from random weights (50B tokens, sequences up to 1,024) Filtered web text, educational and scientific documents, Wikipedia, StackExchange, synthetic question–answer text and code; deduplicated and decontaminated against the MTEB(eng, v2) test sets 2. Contrastive pair training What "related" means (about 20M pairs) Public question–answer, title–body, paraphrase and citation pairs 3. Distillation (short) Light alignment to larger embedding models Teacher-scored public texts 4. Supervised fine-tuning Task skills, with teacher-mined hard negatives Public labelled data for retrieval, NLI, paraphrase, classification and clustering, including MTEB training splits; synthetic training triplets What mattered most: Measuring correctly. Scoring in fp32 and averaging clustering over several seeds removed noise that was larger than the effects we were testing. Matching training and use. Short prompts the model saw in training help; long unseen instructions hurt a mean-pooled model. Choosing data by measurement. Testing pair sources one at a time showed that some popular sources made out-of-domain retrieval worse. Quickstart Sentence Transformers pip install -U sentence-transformers from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer model = SentenceTransformer("harims95/hobbylm-embed-140m", revision="ea708cee107818fa0c1871eebd26d82a1e3fb1aa", trust_remote_code=True) queries = ["how do vaccines work?"] passages = [ "Vaccines train the immune system to recognise a pathogen without causing the disease.", "The Eiffel Tower was completed in 1889.", ] q = model.encode_query(queries) # adds "query: " p = model.encode_document(passages) # adds "passage: " print(q.shape) # (1, 512) print(model.similarity(q, p)) # tensor([[0.6537, 0.2375]]) trust_remote_code=True is required: the MoE encoder is custom code shipped in this repo. encode_query / encode_document (or prompt_name="query" / "passage") add the prompts. Typing them yourself gives the same vector; never do both. For similarity, clustering and classification, use plain model.encode(texts). Embeddings are L2-normalised, so cosine similarity equals the dot product. Long documents (up to 2,048 tokens) model.max_seq_length = 2048 Use it for long-document search (contracts, transcripts, reports). Longer inputs are slower to encode; chunk anything longer than 2,048 tokens. One text per line; texts are stripped. The GGUF files are tested at 512 tokens; their context limit is 1,024 tokens. For long documents (up to 2,048 tokens) use Sentence Transformers with model.max_seq_length = 2048. llama.cpp does not truncate, so shorten longer texts yourself. llama.cpp's built-in mean pooling includes the end-of-text token, so use the helper script for exact embeddings. Ollama's pooling includes the final end-of-text token, so its vectors are close to but not identical with the reference model: on normal sentences cosine is about 0.99 and task scores stay within ±0.4, but very short texts (one or two words) differ most (cosine about 0.92–0.97). HobbyLM-Embed-140M

An English text-embedding model built on a sparse mixture-of-experts encoder, trained from scratch: 140M total parameters, 36M active per token (excluding embeddings), 512-dimensional dense embeddings for search, RAG, similarity, clustering and classification. HobbyLM by Fuel Labs

GGUF | MLX | Demo | Cookbooks | Ollama | GitHub | MTEB

Hugging Face's automatic "Use this model" snippets are not validated for HobbyLM-Embed. Use the snippets on this page, which were tested as written.

亮点

  • Trained from scratch. The encoder started from random weights and was pretrained on 50B tokens. It was not adapted from BERT, ModernBERT or any other existing encoder.
  • Sparse inside, dense outside. Each token runs through 8 of 32 experts in every MoE layer, with 36M parameters active per token, excluding the embedding table. The output is an ordinary dense 512-d vector that works with any vector database.
  • Officially on MTEB. 62.33 on MTEB(eng, v2), all 41 tasks, scored through the loader merged into the mteb package.
  • Reads long documents. 512 tokens by default; set it to 2,048 and long-document search improves from 36.1 to 49.3 nDCG@10 on LongEmbed.
  • Runs where you are. Sentence Transformers on CPU or GPU, LangChain, LlamaIndex and Chroma, llama.cpp (GGUF), Ollama, and MLX on Apple Silicon.
  • 阿帕奇-2.0。 Weights, model code and tools.

介绍

Most small embedding models are adapted from an existing encoder. We wanted to build one end to end: the architecture, the pretraining, every embedding stage and the evaluation. HobbyLM-Embed takes the sparse mixture-of-experts design of the HobbyLM model family, makes its attention bidirectional, and trains it from random weights into a general-purpose English embedding model.

The encoder has 140M total parameters, with 36M active per token excluding embeddings, and produces a 512-dimensional dense vector. It is meant to be practical: it runs on a laptop CPU, plugs into the common RAG frameworks, and has GGUF, Ollama and MLX versions for running locally.

How to read these numbers

  • Retrieval tasks use query: / passage: prompts; every other task uses plain text.
  • Fine-tuning used the training splits of some MTEB tasks (never their test splits), and some training text comes from the same source corpora as some MTEB tasks. All of these are declared in the model's MTEB entry: 26 of 41 tasks, so MTEB lists the model as 36% zero-shot.
  • The final checkpoint was selected using MTEB scores.
  • Treat the benchmark mean as optimistic for domains the model has not seen, and evaluate on your own data.

Long documents

The model reads up to 2,048 tokens when you raise the input length (see Quickstart). On LongEmbed's four real long-document retrieval tasks:

LongEmbed task (nDCG@10) 512 1,024 2,048
NarrativeQA 16.15 16.54 18.16

SummScreenFD 58.41 74.16 84.77
平均的 36.06 43.44 49.33
  • On synthetic tests where one fact is hidden in a 2,048-token document, accuracy@1 rises from 22% to 96% (passkey) and from 24% to 82% (needle). At 512 the model only sees facts in the first 512 tokens.
  • On MTEB(eng, v2) the 40-task mean is unchanged at 2,048 (63.16 → 63.14), but similarity between long news articles (STS22) drops by 1.7 points. That is why 512 stays the default and 2,048 is a one-line option for long-document search.
  • The final fine-tuning stage used inputs of at most 256 tokens; lengths beyond 2,048 are not tested.

Training recipe

Four stages, each starting from the previous one's weights. Data sources are described by type; mixtures, preparation details and training code are not released.

Stage What it teaches Data
1. Masked-token pretraining Language, from random weights (50B tokens, sequences up to 1,024) Filtered web text, educational and scientific documents, Wikipedia, StackExchange, synthetic question–answer text and code; deduplicated and decontaminated against the MTEB(eng, v2) test sets
2. Contrastive pair training What "related" means (about 20M pairs) Public question–answer, title–body, paraphrase and citation pairs
3. Distillation (short) Light alignment to larger embedding models Teacher-scored public texts
4. Supervised fine-tuning Task skills, with teacher-mined hard negatives Public labelled data for retrieval, NLI, paraphrase, classification and clustering, including MTEB training splits; synthetic training triplets

What mattered most:

  • Measuring correctly. Scoring in fp32 and averaging clustering over several seeds removed noise that was larger than the effects we were testing.
  • Matching training and use. Short prompts the model saw in training help; long unseen instructions hurt a mean-pooled model.
  • Choosing data by measurement. Testing pair sources one at a time showed that some popular sources made out-of-domain retrieval worse.

快速入门

Sentence Transformers

pip install -U sentence-transformers

from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer

model = SentenceTransformer("harims95/hobbylm-embed-140m", revision="ea708cee107818fa0c1871eebd26d82a1e3fb1aa",
                            trust_remote_code=True)

queries = ["how do vaccines work?"]
passages = [
    "Vaccines train the immune system to recognise a pathogen without causing the disease.",
    "The Eiffel Tower was completed in 1889.",
]

q = model.encode_query(queries)        # adds "query: "
p = model.encode_document(passages)    # adds "passage: "
print(q.shape)                         # (1, 512)
print(model.similarity(q, p))          # tensor([[0.6537, 0.2375]])
  • trust_remote_code=True is required: the MoE encoder is custom code shipped in this repo.
  • encode_query / encode_document (or prompt_name="query" / "passage") add the prompts. Typing them yourself gives the same vector; never do both.
  • For similarity, clustering and classification, use plain model.encode(texts).
  • Embeddings are L2-normalised, so cosine similarity equals the dot product.

Long documents (up to 2,048 tokens)

model.max_seq_length = 2048

Use it for long-document search (contracts, transcripts, reports). Longer inputs are slower to encode; chunk anything longer than 2,048 tokens.

LangChain, LlamaIndex and Chroma

Every snippet below was run exactly as written on CPU, each in a new virtual environment with an empty Hugging Face cache, with the model pinned to revision ea708cee107818fa0c1871eebd26d82a1e3fb1aa. langchain-hobbylm, LlamaIndex and Chroma give the same vectors as Sentence Transformers (cosine 1.000000 on 2 prompted queries and 2 prompted passages, and on a 5,098-token passage at 2,048 tokens); langchain-huggingface does for single-line text (see its note). As everywhere, queries need query: and documents need passage: . The LlamaIndex and Chroma snippets use these texts (the LangChain snippets define them inline):

QUERIES = ["how do vaccines work?", "what is the capital of france"]
PASSAGES = ["Vaccines train the immune system to recognise a pathogen without causing the disease.",
            "Paris is the capital and largest city of France."]

浪链

Recommended: langchain-hobbylm 0.1.1. It sets the query / passage prompts and pins the model revision for you. Tested 23 Nov 2026 (Linux, Python 3.12.16, new venv, empty Hugging Face cache): langchain-hobbylm 0.1.1, langchain-core 1.8.4, sentence-transformers 6.3.0, transformers 5.24.0, torch 2.15.0, huggingface-hub 2.4.0, numpy 2.5.5.

pip install langchain-hobbylm

from langchain_core.vectorstores import InMemoryVectorStore
from langchain_hobbylm import HobbyLMEmbeddings

embeddings = HobbyLMEmbeddings(revision="ea708cee107818fa0c1871eebd26d82a1e3fb1aa")

queries = ["how do vaccines work?", "what is the capital of france"]
passages = ["Vaccines train the immune system to recognise a pathogen without causing the disease.",
            "Paris is the capital and largest city of France."]

q = [embeddings.embed_query(t) for t in queries]   # "query: " prompt
p = embeddings.embed_documents(passages)           # "passage: " prompt
print("dims", len(q[0]), "norms", [round(sum(x * x for x in v) ** 0.5, 4) for v in q + p])

store = InMemoryVectorStore.from_texts(passages, embedding=embeddings)
for t in queries:
    print(t, "->", store.similarity_search(t, k=1)[0].page_content)

骆驼指数

Tested 23 Nov 2026 in a new venv with an empty Hugging Face cache: llama-index-embeddings-huggingface 0.9.0, llama-index-core 0.14.26, sentence-transformers 6.3.0, transformers 5.24.0, torch 2.15.0, huggingface_hub 2.4.0, numpy 2.5.5, Python 3.12, CPU. LlamaIndex sets its own prompts, so the model's prompts go in query_instruction (queries) and text_instruction (documents). The revision is pinned, so no "new version ... malicious code" warning appears.

pip install llama-index-embeddings-huggingface

                             revision="ea708cee107818fa0c1871eebd26d82a1e3fb1aa",
                             trust_remote_code=True, device="cpu",
                             query_instruction="query: ", text_instruction="passage: ")

p = embed.get_text_embedding_batch(PASSAGES)

print("dims", len(q[0]), "norms", [round(sum(x * x for x in v) ** 0.5, 4) for v in q + p])
for t, v in zip(QUERIES, q):

Chroma

Tested 23 Nov 2026 in a new venv with an empty Hugging Face cache: chromadb 1.5.9, sentence-transformers 6.3.0, transformers 5.24.0, torch 2.15.0, huggingface_hub 2.4.0, numpy 2.5.5, Python 3.12, CPU. Chroma's embedding function has no query/document setting, so the prompts are added to the texts: query: for queries and passage: for documents. The revision is pinned, so no "new version ... malicious code" warning appears.

pip install chromadb sentence-transformers

import chromadb

                                          revision="ea708cee107818fa0c1871eebd26d82a1e3fb1aa",
                                          trust_remote_code=True, device="cpu")

p = ef(["passage: " + t for t in PASSAGES])
print("dims", len(q[0]), "norms", [round(float((v * v).sum()) ** 0.5, 4) for v in q + p])

# end to end: in-memory collection, cosine space
col = chromadb.Client().create_collection("demo", embedding_function=ef, metadata={"hnsw:space": "cosine"})
col.add(ids=["vaccines", "paris"], documents=["passage: " + t for t in PASSAGES])
res = col.query(query_texts=["query: " + t for t in QUERIES], n_results=1)
print("top result per query:", res["ids"])

  • --mode query / --mode passage for retrieval; --mode none for similarity, classification and clustering.
  • One text per line; texts are stripped. The GGUF files are tested at 512 tokens; their context limit is 1,024 tokens. For long documents (up to 2,048 tokens) use Sentence Transformers with model.max_seq_length = 2048. llama.cpp does not truncate, so shorten longer texts yourself.

llama.cpp's built-in mean pooling includes the end-of-text token, so use the helper script for exact embeddings.

The response holds one 512-d, L2-normalised vector per input under "embeddings". As with the other runtimes, prefix retrieval queries with query: and documents with passage: , and use plain text for similarity, clustering and classification. The model runs with num_ctx 512.

Ollama's pooling includes the final end-of-text token, so its vectors are close to but not identical with the reference model: on normal sentences cosine is about 0.99 and task scores stay within ±0.4, but very short texts (one or two words) differ most (cosine about 0.92–0.97). Don't mix Ollama vectors with exact vectors in one index.

Limitations and disclaimer

  • 仅英语。 The GPT-2 tokenizer is also inefficient for code and non-English text.
  • Prompts matter. Retrieval needs query: / passage: ; mixing prompted and unprompted vectors in one index degrades results.
  • Input length. 512 tokens by default; up to 2,048 tested on LongEmbed; longer inputs are slower and nothing beyond 2,048 is tested.
  • Custom code. Loading requires trust_remote_code=True. The reference implementation runs experts in a loop, so batching texts together is much faster than encoding them one at a time.
  • Benchmark context. The MTEB score includes tasks whose training splits were used, and the checkpoint was selected on MTEB. Evaluate on your own data before relying on it.
  • No guarantees. Embeddings can reflect biases in public web and labelled data. The model is provided as is, without warranty.
